activity_context.topic_title: Triple Integrals in Spherical Polar Coordinates

examples.knowledge_point: Rewriting a Triple Integral Defined Over a Shifted Sphere
examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096572/assets/95bb2c41fc54db270b8f6c884767868a8c691372a5d0910109f67582ef361ac6.png)

 

The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere $x^2+y^2+z^2=10x$ for $y \leq 0$ and $z \leq 0,$ shown above.
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
\iiint\limits_R \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}} \:\textrm{d}V
$$
examples.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = 
\iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(\rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \rho\cos\phi) \:  \rho^2\sin\phi \: \mathrm{d}\rho \, \mathrm{d}\theta \, \mathrm{d}\phi.
$$

If $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad
y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad 
z = \rho\cos\phi
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-quarter of the sphere of radius $5$ centered at $(5,0,0).$

With that in mind, let's now write the $x^2+y^2+z^2=10x$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =10x \\ {\rho }^{2} & =10\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\ \rho (\rho -10\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $\rho$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =10\cos\theta\sin\phi.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096572/assets/53c68b2181ffbc7bd4a47206f67ee3da2af19d5f80683fd5ecb367c7d57bd47a.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (\rho, \theta, \phi) \, : \, 0 \leq \rho \leq 10\cos\theta\sin\phi, \:\dfrac{3\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq 2\pi , \: \dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq \phi \leq \pi \right\}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\frac{1}{\rho }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{1}{\rho }\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{10\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=4$ for $x\le 0.$
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}V
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-half of the sphere of radius $2$ centered at the origin.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096572/assets/de9f30a4f54875e05a8cedb6c73af37ad7146c56ab62d0b2b2d3f3fa359160ca.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 2,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2},\,0\le ϕ\le \pi }.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}+(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2} \\  & ={\rho }^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ+{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ \\  & ={\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\rho }^{4}{sin}^{3}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$
